newsitem.title: UK: Britain still mulling BA-American deal.
newsitem.headline: Britain still mulling BA-American deal.

text.p: Britain's Office of Fair Trading said on Tuesday it has not yet ruled on whether British Airways' controversial alliance plans with American Airlines should be referred to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
The plans by BA and American have attracted fierce criticism from rival airlines as well as consumer groups, who say the alliance will dominate the London trans-Atlantic market.

The OFT is due to report to British trade minister Ian Lang on the findings of its three-month preliminary investigation into the deal and advise him on whether or not the proposed deal should be referred to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission for a full inquiry.
Industry sources said there is some speculation that Lang will get the long awaited report on Friday, which means there is unlikely to be any public announcements before next week, at the earliest.
"It has not happened yet," said a spokesman for the OFT. "Our advice has not been passed yet (to Lang)."
He declined to say when the report might be published but noted that Lang was likely to need some time to consider the OFT's findings before announcing his verdict.
Lang's Department of Trade and Industry also confirmed the OFT had not reported back yet but declined to comment further.
"Generally the Secretary of State (Lang) likes to make an announcement as soon as possible," a department official said.
"He will have to consider it (the OFT report) first, obviously," she added.

Under the alliance, BA intends to coordinate its 244 flights a week from Britain to 22 U.S. destinations with all of American's 238 flights a week from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.
They would also combine their frequent flyer programmes and share flight booking codes to promote their connecting flights on computer reservation systems.

BA and American argue that their deal will lead to greater competition on transatlantic routes because it will only go ahead if Britain and the U.S. liberalise the market with an "open skies" trade pact.

They also say they must be allowed to combine to defend their own positions against rival alliances such as that between United Airlines and Germany's Lufthansa in competing for all-important transfer traffic.
But "open skies" talks between government negotiators broke down last month "and nothing more seems to have been scheduled," bemoaned one industry source on Tuesday.
American's chairman Robert Crandall was in Britain this week lobbying newspapers and politicians, including deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine, whom he saw on Monday.
"He is meeting with a number of business, political and media representatives to explain American's view of the proposed alliance with BA," a company spokesman said.
The head of American's arch rival United Airlines, Gerald Greenwald,is also visiting London this week, to speak at an American Chamber of Commerce lunch on Thursday.
"The BA/American proposals will obviously be a talking point," a spokesman for Greenwald said.
